notes:
I couldn't cover the whole passage. Several sources failed to load, and I ran out of searches and page fetches. Enduring Word, Precept Austin, Ellicott's full chapter, Gill's full chapter, and the Catholic, Orthodox, Pentecostal, Lutheran-site and Reformed-site pages are all missing. The best coverage is for vv. 26–30, 35, 45, 49 and 50. For vv. 31–34 I only have one brief summary, and for vv. 36–44 and 46–48 I have almost nothing. I left those gaps empty rather than fill them from memory.

The Pulpit Commentary page I read in full doesn't support exact citations, so for those points I give the link and summarise in my own words. Its text on v. 30 is cut off partway through.

---

**v. 26**
- **Traditional reading (Pulpit Commentary):** God treats people the way they treat Him. The verb for "crooked/froward" deliberately differs from the adjective. God can't actually *be* crooked; He only shows Himself opposed to the crooked. They act perversely, but He acts justly. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- The Pulpit's sermon notes make a general rule of it: "What God is to you—what Christ is to you, shows what you are, and determines what you shall be." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 27**
- **Pulpit:** The "afflicted" are the oppressed, and they are assumed to be godly. The verse is about God bringing down the proud. Pagan writers like Herodotus noticed this too, but they thought God was envious of the proud, which the Bible does not say. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- **Pulpit sermon notes:** "The gospel is an open secret, but still a secret, from proud, worldly hearts. The physician is for those who are sick and know it. The Saviour is for sinners who feel themselves sinners." https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**v. 28**
- **Pulpit:** The word is "lamp," the same word used for the tabernacle lampstand. David himself is called "the lamp of Israel" in 2 Sam 21:17. The real light was the light of God's face. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- **Constable:** God kept the lamp of David's life burning by delivering his life from the hands of his enemies. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-28.html
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** God brings a person out of darkness into light, either out of adversity to prosperity, or from walking in darkness to the enjoyment of the light of his countenance. Gill also applies the verse to Christ, who was in darkness on the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-28.html

**v. 29**
- **Pulpit:** The "troop" (*gedud*) is a raiding band, like the Amalekites David chased after Ziklag was burned (1 Sam 30). The "wall" may refer to David taking Zion from the Jebusites. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html
- **Constable:** God enabled His servant to advance against his foes and to overcome their defenses. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-28.html

**v. 30**
- **Pulpit (compare Deut 32:4):** God does nothing by halves. "Tried/flawless" means His promises have been tested as if by fire and will never fail. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**vv. 31–34**
- **Bridgeway (only source found):** God had blessed David with good health, physical strength, natural ability, and the desire to train and practise till he was skilled in the abilities God had given him (31-34). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-2.html

**v. 35**
- **Shield and right hand (Barnes):** God threw His shield in front of David in danger, and held him up when he was about to fall. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-35.htm
- **"Gentleness" (Barnes):** Used of God, the word means mildness, clemency, favour. David owed his success wholly because God had dealt kindly with him, not to any worth or strength of his own. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-35.htm
- **Pulpit (via Bible Hub):** The word means "condescension," the quality in God closest to humility in a person. The word is not elsewhere used of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-35.htm
- **Ellicott:** The verse foreshadows Jesus' "I am meek and lowly." He asks "Why be afraid to speak of the Divine Being as meek any more than as jealous." https://biblehub.com/psalms/18-35.htm
- **Where traditions differ on "gentleness":**
  - *Lutheran:* Luther followed the Greek and Latin versions, translating "When Thou humblest me, Thou makest me great." Keil and Delitzsch object that the Hebrew word means bending oneself, not bending someone else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-35.htm
  - *Anglican:* The older English version kept in the Prayer Book has a similar sense, "Thy loving correction shall make me great." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/hastings/psalms/18-35.htm
  - *Methodist (Adam Clarke):* Clarke reads it as God's meekness working in David. God enabled me to bear and forbear; to behave with courage in adversity, and with humility in prosperity; and thus I am become great. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/psalms/18-35.html
  - *Baptist (Gill):* David's greatness was not owing to his merits, but to the providential goodness of God. Gill also mentions the reading "thy humility," meaning God stooping to look on David in his low state. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-35.htm
  - *Baptist (Spurgeon):* David gratefully ascribed all his greatness not to his own goodness, but to the goodness of God. Spurgeon applies this to believers' election in Christ. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/divine-gentleness-acknowledged/
- **Catholic tradition (the Latin Vulgate, as reported by Clarke; I couldn't read a Catholic site):** The Vulgate has "And thy discipline itself shall teach me." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-35.html
- **Modern scholarship (NET note):** The phrase refers to God's willingness to answer prayer. one might translate, "your favorable response." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=psa&chapter=18&verse=35

**vv. 37–42**
- **Bridgeway (only source):** With God's help David went on to certain victory, conquering his foes (37-42). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-2.html

**vv. 43–45**
- **Bridgeway:** These verses describe David expanding his kingdom (43-45). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-2.html
- **v. 45, Pulpit (reading it about Christ's kingdom):** Converts are represented as coming into the Church, not merely from love, but partly from fear. The kingdom of the Redeemer at once attracts and alarms. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

**vv. 46–48**
- **Bridgeway:** These verses are about bringing glory to God (46-48). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/18-2.html

**v. 49**
- **Pulpit:** David was in some sense "head of the nations" (v. 43), so he should praise God among them and lead them toward the true God by example. sing praises unto thy Name; i.e. to thy Person - God being in his Name. https://biblehub.com/psalms/18-49.htm
- **Spurgeon:** Paul's quotation in Rom 15:9 shows David's Lord is here, but David is here too, and is to be viewed as an example of a holy soul making its boast in God even in the presence of ungodly men. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps018.cfm
- **Clarke** quotes Theodoret, an early Church Father: David still praises God among the nations whenever Christians anywhere sing his psalms. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/18-49.html
- **Commentators differ on how far this verse is a prophecy:**
  - *Barnes:* Paul uses the verse to mean the Gentiles would join Israel in praise, but this does not appear to have been the original design of David in the psalm. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/15-9.html
  - *Clarke:* Paul quotes it to prove that the calling of the Gentiles was predicted. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/psalms/18-49.html
  - *Matthew Poole:* David speaks this in the person of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/15-9.htm

**v. 50**
- **Barnes:** There is an undoubted reference here to the promises made to David in regard to his successors on the throne. David's earthly line came to an end, but the spiritual reign is perpetual in the Messiah. How much David himself understood of this can't be known. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-50.htm
- **Poole:** "His seed" means all his descendants, and especially to the Messias, who is called David's Seed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-50.htm
- **Matthew Henry:** If we belong to Him, we shall conquer and reign through him, and partake of the mercy of our anointed King. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/18-50.htm
- **Pulpit:** The closing "forever" stretches across the whole present age, looking ahead to Christ having all enemies under His feet. Revelation 5 can be read as the psalm's sequel. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-18.html

---

**Not found:** I found no material on Orthodox or Catholic readings beyond the Vulgate note, and none from the Pentecostal sites. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace use of these verses (vv. 29, 32–35 would be the obvious ones). Apart from v. 35, I found no clear disagreements between Protestant traditions. Next time, I'd look first at Enduring Word, Precept Austin and Ellicott for the missing verses (31–34, 36–48).
